title: Why black radio arrived: black press images, race records and Elvis
summary: Blacks saw stars in the black papers but rarely heard them; white DJs called such records race records, and black radio brought them closer.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: All right, well. I'm sorry. Let me ask a question. I had a broader question I was going to get back to WMR. Why do you think, finally, at this point in time, that there is black radio, finally? All right.

All right. You've got to remember. Now, we started talking about the black newspapers. The three black newspapers we had, the Informer Sentinel, La Courier, and Louisiana Wheeler, showed pictures of Conk Basie, Duke Ellington, Jimmy Liggins, Billy Eckstein, Joe Lewis. Image factors that blacks could look up to. Sure. But they had never seen these people. They've only rarely heard them. See, you didn't have jukeboxes. You had jukeboxes, but they were just beginning to highlight the black intelligentsia and entertainment. All right. But we wanted to see them, and we wanted to hear more about them. Remember, in the 1940s and the early 50s, white disc jockeys, whenever they picked up a record by Louis Armstrong, a Conk Basie or Duke Ellington, they said race records. They didn't say rock and roll. Rock and roll didn't come along until Elvis Presley started shaking his hips, you see. So that was the difference. But eventually, here's what made it much better for us. In the little areas like down in Plaquemines Parish, like in St. Bernard, like over in Jefferson, the West Bank of the River, in West Regal, moreover, people wanted to see what they were doing, and the other people wanted to see what they looked like. We wanted to be there with them. We wanted to give them support. And the biggest problem was trying to stay away from women. That was a good-looking kid with Indian-type features, cold black curly hair. He looked like a black Indian. He's a very handsome man. Well, myself, I don't want to brag, but I felt to believe that I had a certain type of physical qualities in my early 20s that sort of gave me a certain type of splendor in order to deal with life and with people, to extol my virtues and pass them on to somebody and say that I'm a gentleman of quality. Sure. Well, of course you are. So I did that.
